result: A novel FRET-based assay was developed to monitor in real time both GTase and TPase reactions of class A PBPs reconstituted in liposomes or supported lipid bilayers. The assay was successfully applied to PBP1B homologues from E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii in the presence or absence of their cognate lipoprotein activators.
evaluation: Claims C4 and C5 describe the main methodological contribution of the manuscript. The development and application of the FRET assay is extensively supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript (Figures 1-5 and supplementary figures), demonstrating its functionality across multiple bacterial species and conditions.

result: Fluorescently labeled lipid II (Atto550 and Atto647n) is incorporated into PG by PBP1BEc, resulting in FRET that depends on both GTase and TPase activity, with TPase being the major contributor. FRET efficiency was 29±6%, which was reduced to one-third by ampicillin (TPase inhibitor) and abolished by moenomycin (GTase inhibitor).
evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1B-D showing incorporation of both fluorescent probes, FRET signal generation, and differential effects of specific inhibitors. The quantitative FRET efficiency measurements and the clear demonstration of antibiotic effects provide strong evidence for the conclusion that TPase is the major contributor to FRET.

result: Real-time monitoring of PBP1BEc activity in detergents showed that without LpoB, FRET appeared after ~5 min and plateaued after 50-60 min, while with LpoB(sol), FRET increased immediately and plateaued after 10-20 min. LpoB increased reaction slopes approximately 10- or 20-fold in the absence or presence of ampicillin, respectively. Moenomycin abolished FRET, while ampicillin reduced it threefold.
evaluation: Claims C34-C38 and C41 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1E-F showing real-time FRET curves and quantified slopes. The data clearly demonstrate the activating effect of LpoB and the differential effects of antibiotics, with appropriate controls and quantification.

result: Digestion experiments with MepM (endopeptidase) and cellosyl (muramidase) demonstrated that inter-chain FRET is a major contributor to the total FRET signal. MepM reduced FRET efficiency by approximately twofold for crosslinked PG but had negligible effect on glycan chains produced with ampicillin. Cellosyl completely abolished FRET for both products. FRET correlated with formation of crosslinked muropeptide dimers, not lipid II consumption rate.
evaluation: Claims C43-C50 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-E showing the effects of enzymatic digestion on FRET and correlation with HPLC analysis of products. The differential effects of MepM (which cleaves crosslinks) versus cellosyl (which cleaves glycan chains) provide strong evidence for the conclusion that inter-chain FRET dominates the signal.

result: PBP1BEc alone could not polymerize fluorescently labeled lipid II without unlabeled lipid II, but addition of LpoB enabled production of short, non-crosslinked chains with slow but large FRET increase. Experiments varying the proportion of fluorescent lipid II showed that LpoB stimulates incorporation of fluorophores in consecutive positions along glycan chains, increasing intra-chain FRET contribution. The increase in reaction slopes with activator reflects both higher PG synthesis rate and higher intra-chain FRET contribution.
evaluation: Claims C51-C60 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, showing the requirement for unlabeled lipid II, the effect of LpoB on polymerization of labeled substrates, and systematic variation of fluorescent lipid II proportions. The data provide strong evidence for the conclusion about LpoB's effect on intra-chain FRET, though the interpretation involves some inference about the mechanism.

result: PBP1BEc was successfully reconstituted in liposomes with the N-terminus inside, as demonstrated by accessibility assays. The liposome-reconstituted enzyme required absence of NaCl for improved activity and showed slower reaction rates than detergent-solubilized enzyme, with longer lag times. LpoB(sol) produced approximately tenfold increase in initial slope and much higher final FRET. Both fluorescent probes were incorporated into PG products in liposomes.
evaluation: Claims C61-C72 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-C and supplementary figures showing protein orientation, activity requirements, and FRET measurements in liposomes. The data demonstrate successful reconstitution and functional activity, though the slower rates in liposomes compared to detergents suggest some limitations of the system.

result: A hypothetical lipoprotein (LpoPAb) containing two tetratricopeptide repeats was identified next to the PBP1BAb gene and found to activate PBP1BAb. LpoPAb(sol) stimulated PBP1BAb GTase activity ~3.3-fold and accelerated lipid II consumption and glycan chain polymerization.
evaluation: Claims C73-C78 are supported by bioinformatic analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 6) showing identification and functional characterization of LpoPAb. The discovery of a novel activator for A. baumannii PBP1B is well-supported by the data.

result: PBP1BAb showed low FRET signal and poor crosslinked PG production in detergents, but displayed higher TPase activity in liposomes with substantially higher final FRET signal. Ampicillin had negligible effect in detergents and only small effect in liposomes (~1.2-fold reduction), indicating intra-chain FRET is the major contributor. LpoPAb(sol) stimulated PBP1BAb more strongly in detergents (12.3-fold) than liposomes (~2.5-fold).
evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3E-F and supplementary figures showing differential activity of PBP1BAb in detergents versus liposomes. The data demonstrate that membrane environment significantly affects enzyme activity, with important implications for understanding physiological function.

result: PBP1BPa displayed robust TPase activity in both detergents and liposomes. Ampicillin reduced final FRET by ~1.8-fold in detergents and ~1.5-fold in liposomes, indicating substantial inter-chain FRET contribution. LpoPPa(sol) increased final FRET ~2-fold and accelerated initial slopes ~4-11-fold, with increased lipid II consumption under both conditions, indicating stimulation of both GTase and TPase activities.
evaluation: Claims C85-C90 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3G-H and supplementary figures showing PBP1BPa activity in different environments and the effects of LpoPPa. The data are consistent with a recent report (Caveney et al., 2020) and demonstrate that the FRET assay can detect dual activation of both enzymatic activities.

result: Single PBP1BEc molecules reconstituted in supported lipid bilayers could be tracked by TIRF microscopy. PBP1BEc diffused with average Dcoef of 0.23±0.06 µm²/s, which decreased to 0.10±0.06 µm²/s upon addition of lipid II. Prolonged confined motion was not detected, but average displacement length between frames was reduced.
evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4B-E and Video 1 showing single-molecule tracking of fluorescently labeled PBP1BEc. The data demonstrate successful reconstitution at low density and provide quantitative measurements of diffusion changes upon substrate addition, supporting the interpretation that substrate binding slows enzyme diffusion.

result: SLB-reconstituted PBP1BEc incorporated about 12% of added radiolabeled lipid II into PG after overnight incubation with LpoB(sol). HPLC analysis revealed production of both GTase and TPase products that were absent with moenomycin. About 32% of radioactivity remained in membrane fraction after washing, with no PG products in wash fraction, confirming PG synthesis occurred on SLBs and remained attached. PBP1BEc did not affect lipid II binding to bilayer.
evaluation: Claims C98-C103 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing radioactive lipid II incorporation and HPLC analysis of products. The data demonstrate that PBP1BEc remains active on SLBs and produces membrane-attached PG, though the low incorporation efficiency (12%) suggests limitations of the system at very low enzyme density.

result: FRET was detected on SLBs by acceptor photobleaching after addition of unlabeled lipid II and LpoB(sol), with signal increasing after ~8 min lag phase. No FRET increase occurred with ampicillin, GTase-defective PBP1BEc (E233Q), or after cellosyl digestion, indicating the FRET signal is primarily due to transpeptidase activity.
evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C and supplementary figures showing FRET detection by microscopy with appropriate controls. The multiple lines of evidence (ampicillin inhibition, GTase mutant, cellosyl digestion) strongly support the conclusion that TPase activity is the primary contributor to FRET on SLBs.

result: During PG synthesis on SLBs, the diffusion coefficient of lipid II-Atto647n decreased 2-3-fold in a time-dependent manner when crosslinking was permitted (no ampicillin), reaching minimum at ~10 min similar to FRET lag. The immobile fraction did not change significantly (13±2% vs 18±6% with/without ampicillin, p=0.15). Ampicillin only affected lipid II diffusivity (2.9±0.4 vs 0.67±0.1 µm²/s), not membrane lipid probe diffusivity (1.6±0.65 vs 1.94±0.62 µm²/s), indicating lipid II was incorporated into small groups of crosslinked glycan chains that remain mobile.
evaluation: Claims C110-C117 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-F showing FRAP analysis of lipid II and membrane probe diffusion during PG synthesis. The data provide strong evidence that crosslinked PG remains mobile on SLBs but diffuses more slowly, with appropriate controls demonstrating membrane fluidity is not affected by the synthesis reaction.

result: For all PBPs tested, FRET increased with GTase activity alone (intra-chain FRET) but was always higher with active TPase (inter-chain FRET). For PBP1BEc, FRET curves closely followed crosslinked PG production rate and decreased substantially upon endopeptidase digestion, indicating inter-chain FRET is a main component. The authors hypothesize that TPase brings glycan chains into close proximity, reducing probe distances to produce high FRET, possibly because steric constraints prevent incorporation of two large fluorescent lipid II molecules at successive positions in a single chain.
evaluation: Claims C118-C122, C124-C125 summarize key findings about FRET mechanisms supported by data in Figures 1-3 and supplementary figures. The conclusion that inter-chain FRET dominates is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence (antibiotic effects, enzymatic digestion, HPLC correlation). The hypothesis about steric constraints (C122) is speculative but reasonable given the data and prior work (Van't Veer et al., 2016).

result: The overall FRET signal combines intra-chain and inter-chain FRET, which depend on average distances and orientation of fluorophores on growing glycan chains. There is currently no method to measure these parameters individually, preventing determination of absolute GTase and TPase rates. Different PBPs may produce different fluorophore distributions, and activators can enhance incorporation of fluorescent lipid II analogues. The assay is inherently semi-quantitative, but with appropriate controls it can determine whether FRET follows more the GTase or TPase reaction.
evaluation: Claims C126-C130 accurately describe the limitations of the FRET assay. These are honest assessments supported by the experimental observations (e.g., C129 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The authors appropriately acknowledge that the assay is semi-quantitative while demonstrating its utility for comparative studies.

result: All three PBP1B homologues (E. coli, P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii) started reactions after a lag phase that was abolished by cognate activators. The authors suggest this slow start and its acceleration by Lpo activators could be an important mechanism to initiate PG synthesis at gaps in the PG layer where activators can contact the synthase.
evaluation: Claim C132 is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work showing the lag phase and activator effects. Claim C133 is speculative but reasonable given recent work on PBP1B's role in cell wall repair (Vigouroux et al., 2020; Morè et al., 2019). The speculation is appropriately presented as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.

result: The authors critique a recent report (Catherwood et al., 2020) that concluded LpoB-mediated TPase activation explains LpoB essentiality, noting that assay used enzyme concentrations too low to support GTase activity without LpoB. They propose an alternative explanation: LpoB essentiality is explained by >10-fold GTase stimulation, and activation by LpoB was much more needed when PBP1B was membrane-embedded compared to detergent-solubilized. In vitro, LpoB also stimulated TPase, producing hyper-crosslinked PG, as observed for LpoPPa and PBP1BPa.
evaluation: Claims C135-C140 present a critique of prior work and alternative interpretation supported by the current data and citations. The critique (C136) is valid and supported by prior work (Pazos et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2007). The alternative explanation (C137-C138) is well-supported by the experimental data showing stronger LpoB requirement in membrane environments. Claims C139-C140 are supported by citations to prior work.

result: Slower reaction rates were found in liposomes than detergents for all enzymes tested. Several factors could explain this (slow lipid II incorporation, limited liposome capacity, undecaprenyl pyrophosphate accumulation), but none should change with LpoB. The authors favor the explanation that membrane-embedding of PBP1B hinders lipid II binding, slowing the reaction.
evaluation: Claim C143 is supported by experimental data comparing detergent and liposome conditions. Claims C144-C146 present possible explanations, with C144 supported by citation to prior work on undecaprenyl pyrophosphate inhibition. The preferred explanation (C146) is speculative but reasonable given the data, particularly the observation that LpoB effects differ between environments.

result: PBP1BAb showed higher TPase activity in liposomes than detergents, highlighting that detergents can affect membrane protein activity and that experimental conditions in PG synthesis assays should be as close as possible to physiological conditions.
evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3E and supplementary figures showing differential activity of PBP1BAb in different environments. This observation reinforces the importance of the membrane-reconstituted assay system and is an important finding for the field.

result: FRET signal increase was detected on SLBs upon triggering PG synthesis, correlating with transpeptidation. Diffusion of reaction products could be followed, indicating PBP1BEc produced smaller patches of crosslinked glycan chains rather than completely covering surfaces with PG. This is attributed to very low PBP1BEc density required to ensure SLB homogeneity and stability.
evaluation: Claims C149-C151 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing FRET detection and product diffusion on SLBs. The interpretation that small patches are produced (C150) is reasonable given the low enzyme density (C151) and the observation that products remain mobile. This is an important finding demonstrating the assay's capability for spatial analysis.

result: A reduction of PBP1BEc diffusivity was detected in the presence of lipid II. Previous in vivo single-molecule tracking reported two populations (fast diffusing and almost immobile), with the immobile population assumed to be active. The current result supports this interpretation, though more experiments are needed.
evaluation: Claim C152 is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing reduced diffusion upon lipid II addition. Claims C153-C154 appropriately connect this finding to prior in vivo work (Cho et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; Vigouroux et al., 2020) while acknowledging the need for further validation. The support for the prior interpretation is reasonable but appropriately cautious.

result: Important advantages of the new assay include use of natural transpeptidation substrates (nascent glycan strands) instead of pentapeptide mimics, and ability to measure activities in natural lipid environment. The assay can potentially be adopted to study PG synthases with interacting proteins (monofunctional PBPs with GTases, interacting class A PBPs) and for high-throughput screening for new antimicrobials.
evaluation: Claims C158-C159 accurately describe advantages of the assay that are demonstrated by the experimental data. Claims C160-C161 are speculative about future applications but reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities of the assay. The speculation is appropriately presented as potential rather than established capability.

result: Background claims about peptidoglycan structure and function: PG is an essential component of the bacterial cell envelope composed of glycan strands of alternating GlcNAc and MurNAc residues interconnected by short peptides, forming a mesh-like layer that protects cells from osmotic lysis and maintains cell shape. Class A PBPs are bifunctional synthases that polymerize glycan chains and crosslink peptides. Important antibiotics target PG biosynthesis.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C6-C7 present established knowledge about peptidoglycan and class A PBPs, supported by the citation to Vollmer et al., 2008 for C7. These are accurate statements of background knowledge that provide context for the study.

result: Background claims about PBP inhibitors, regulation, and lipid II synthesis: Moenomycin inhibits GTase and β-lactams inhibit TPase function of class A PBPs. In E. coli, PBP1A and PBP1B account for substantial PG synthesis activity and are regulated by multiple proteins including LpoA and LpoB. Lipid II can be synthesized chemically, semi-enzymatically, or isolated from cells with inactivated MurJ.
evaluation: Claims C8-C15 present established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These provide important background for understanding the experimental system and are accurately stated.

result: Background claims about limitations of existing PG synthesis assays: Most current assays are end-point assays that don't provide real-time information, involve laborious techniques incompatible with high-throughput screening, or exclusively report on either GTase or TPase but not both. Many include detergents and/or high DMSO concentrations that affect enzyme activity. Detergent-solubilized enzymes have very different environment compared to membrane-confined enzymes.
evaluation: Claims C16-C26 accurately describe limitations of existing methods, supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims establish the rationale for developing the new FRET assay and are well-supported by the literature.
